wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
camps: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: Just under five miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed pass junction, then a couple of miles and roughly two thousand feet through forest and meadow to the gap. The Boulder Creek side reaches the same pass but is far longer now that the road below it is walked or ridden.
hazards: Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully where several holds are vegetation
Narrow goat ramp on the final approach to the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and basin slopes
Snow near the pass and in the basin below the summit into July
Braided, unmarked climbers' path that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
Remote backcountry with unreliable cell coverage, long carry-out
Black bear activity in the drainages; scented items need an approved canister
wa_mount_appleton_standard.baseFinding: Appleton Pass is a true gap with scattered tent pads just below it and maintained trail running on north toward Boulder Lake and east toward Oyster Lake. Leave the tread at the gap and take the climbers' path north along the ridge crest. The base of the real scrambling is a rock step at about 5,800 ft, and the way you know it is a distinct rock horn standing on its south, or left, side — that horn is the marker, and there is nothing else like it on the crest. Below the step you have been on easy heather with a talus basin crossed on the north flank near 5,400 ft; above it you are on exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully and ledge system. Minor outcrops lower on the crest can be turned on either side and are not the step, so do not stop at the first thing that makes you use hands. The narrow goat ramp people talk about comes after the horn, not before it. If you are still traversing level ground with the basin below and no horn in view, you are too low; the notch below the true summit sits near 6,000 ft between the peak's two rocky humps.

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Boulder Creek from the Elwha

bivy.name: Appleton Pass
bivy.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
bivy.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

approachLogistics.trailhead: Boulder Creek Trailhead (Olympic Hot Springs Road)

wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: From the Elwha side, follow the Boulder Creek trail past the old hot springs and climb to Appleton Pass, where it meets the Sol Duc line. It is the longer way, since the road below the trailhead may have to be walked or biked. Boulder Lake makes a good side camp.
hazards: Longer approach since the road below the Boulder Creek trailhead may have to be walked or biked
Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully above Appleton Pass with vegetation holds
Narrow goat ramp near the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge
Lingering snow near the pass and in the basin into July
Braided climbers' path above the pass that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
Remote with unreliable cell coverage; black bear activity in the drainages

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail; the path is often lost
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
wa_mount_ballard_south.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 4,440 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: South Fork Slate Creek road end (over Harts Pass)

wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: Steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
wa_mount_ballard_south.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: Up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips.
hazards: Long approach up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side
Slide alder and downed timber on the unmaintained Mill Creek approach
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Full lightning exposure; very remote with a long, difficult evacuation

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
camps: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: This peak has two genuinely different journeys to it: the western one from the Sol Duc over the High Divide and along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, and the eastern one up the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Both take days. Almost every ascent is a side-summit off a traverse rather than a trip in its own right.
hazards: Days of off-trail travel along the Bailey crest with no quick bail-out and no cell coverage
Firm snow on the small glacier below Bear Pass: axe and traction needed
Few reliable water sources beyond Heart Lake on the long crest traverse
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
Steep scree and lingering snow patches on the contour to the summit scree slope
Deep interior isolation; a high self-rescue burden with helicopter evacuations recorded
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.baseFinding: Bear Pass is a broad saddle marking the southeastern end of the Bailey Range proper, and from it the ground drops into a flat meadow before the mountain itself. Cross the meadow and contour southeast over scree and lingering snow patches until you are southwest of the summit. That position is the base, and you will know it from the change underfoot: the sidehill traversing stops and the slope above turns into a straight fall-line of moderate, evenly sized scree with a boot track curling left, to the north, onto it. Aside from one brief patch of brush the terrain here is open and the top is in view, so the navigation problem is behind you once you are on that track. Decoys: the ridge running east off Bear Pass is not the summit ridge, and the first obvious scree fan you meet while still traversing leads onto broken ground short of the peak. If the boot track has stopped curling north and you are dropping toward the Queets side, you have gone past the turn.

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Up the Elwha to Elwha Basin

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, Mount Barnes, Mount Noyes and Mount Queets are all short days, Mount Meany is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts Mount Ferry and Mount Pulitzer within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and cross-country zones cannot be booked online — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: The eastern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the full length of the valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp to Elwha Basin, then climb onto the peak from the basin. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.
hazards: 'The maze': dense slide-alder bushwhacking between the Elwha River and Elwha Basin that can take hours
The Elwha Snowfinger has largely melted out; expect steep scree, crumbly slabs and an icy snow hump instead of a ramp
Hazardous fords on the upper Elwha in high water
Closed road adds a 6-7 mile walk or bike ride each way before the trail even starts
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
Committing multi-day access in deep interior with a high self-rescue burden

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
Exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
Loose scree and rockfall in the south-west basin and gully
North and west faces are cliffy; going straight up from High Pass does not work
Short fourth-class step to the true north summit
Steep snow and moat on the snow finger in early season (June-early July)
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.baseFinding:
The base is a broad saddle on the south side at about 7,650 ft, and the way you get to it is a snow finger rather than a slope. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a snow finger and its moat, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

The saddle is where the route leaves the basin. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

The negative marker is the most important thing on this peak and it is about aspect: Berge's north and west faces are cliffy. Parties must stay on the south-west side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

The route-finding rule lower down is a descending traverse, which feels wrong and is right: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

The last obstacle has an elevation and a character: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with slanted slabs and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

The summit is not one point. The true, north summit needs a short fourth-class step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

approachLogistics.trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go; this approach passes beneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on the Buck Creek approach
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
Exposed scrambling to gain the narrow 7,840 ft notch in the ridge crest
Loose scree and rockfall in the south-west basin and gully
Exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft on the final climb
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, lengthening the drive-in to Trinity
Remote country, 15+ miles round trip, usually multi-day
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.baseFinding:
The High Pass approach delivers you to the wrong side of the mountain on purpose, and the rule is that you must keep going around. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. The climb is on the south-west side. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

The arrival is the same place for every approach to this peak: the broad saddle on Berge's south side at about 7,650 ft, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

The approach-specific marker on the High Pass line is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

The 7,840 ft notch is the link between the two sides and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

And the same summit warning applies: the true summit is the north one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Eagle Lakes Trail #431 to Upper Eagle Lake
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the forest-road spur, fill out the self-issue wilderness permit and start up Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The tread crosses Crater Creek on a bridge early on — stay straight where the Crater Creek Trail splits — and climbs steadily, with an established camp roughly halfway. Past an overlook of the lower lake the trail reaches a junction: the left branch goes to the lower lake and the pass beyond, the right-hand spur climbs a half mile to Upper Eagle Lake. Take the spur. The upper lake sits in a cirque with established campsites and is the last reliable water and the staging point before the off-trail push, which starts from its northwest shore.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.season: Roughly July through October, once road and trail are snow-free. Snow lingers in the notch through the lower cliff band into summer and makes the route-finding harder.
hazards: Route-finding through the cliff bands is genuinely tricky, especially with snow still lying in the notch
Steep, loose scree and rock between the bands, with a loose path worn straight up it
Pushing too far climber's right onto the better rock cliffs you out at the end of the ridge
An eight-foot chimney below the summit block with poor handholds in small pebbles and sand — a slip there would be serious
The summit rises over 1,300 ft above the upper lake in about a third of a mile
No water above the lake
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.baseFinding: Go up through the larches and veer right to the notch, then cut left under the next band. From Upper Eagle Lake a path runs round the lake; above it the landmark is vegetation rather than rock. Climb up through the larch stand and veer right to a notch, then take easy slabby rock to get above the lower cliff band. Once above it, head left, staying beneath the next band, and only when past that is it a straight push up steep scree and rock to just below the summit block. That alternation — right through the larches, then left under the upper band — is the shape of the route, and the error parties actually make is the opposite: the better, more stable rock lies further climber's right and tempts parties onto it, where they get cliffed out at the end of the ridge and have to downclimb. At the block itself, look for a notch with a chimney step of about eight feet and a sandy gully above it. The step is climbed upward and its top holds are poor, in small pebbles and sand; there is an easier scramble round to the left at its base that rejoins the sandy gully just above the chimney, and taking it is the difference between a committing move and a walk.

wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.name: Horsehead Pass and the west slopes
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.notes: The easier alternative stays on the main trail past the Upper Eagle Lake spur, continues to the lower lake and climbs to Horsehead Pass, then gains the peak's west slopes from the far side of the crest. It trades the exposed scrambling for distance and a long, loose walk-up, and is the sensible choice for a party that does not want the cliff-band route-finding or that finds snow still lying in the notch above the upper lake.
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.season: July through October. The west side melts out and stays passable later in the autumn than the shaded notch on the east side.
hazards: Long and described as annoyingly loose underfoot for its whole length
No water once you leave the lake basin
Exposed crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
wa_mount_bigelow_scramble.baseFinding: This line is identified by what it does not have: no cliff bands and no scrambling. Carry on past the spur to the upper lake, stay on the main trail to the lower lake, and climb to Horsehead Pass on the crest. From the pass the peak's west slopes rise as continuous open scree and broken rock with a walkable line the whole way and nothing that needs hands. That is the confirmation you are on the right side of the mountain. If you find yourself traversing beneath a band of slabby rock, threading a notch, or looking at a short exposed step down into a sandy gully, you have ended up on the direct line from the upper lake instead and should reconsider whether the party is equipped for it. The west slopes are looser and longer than they look from the pass, so the trade is real: this variant removes the scrambling and adds a great deal of tedious ground.

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road
camps: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: Up Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road off the Cascade River Road, then south through the Buckindy high country to below the north side. A longer two-to-three-day approach.
hazards: Notoriously thick slide alder, devil's club and old-growth deadfall in the Kindy Creek drainage
Small glaciers (Kindy and Goat Creek) on the massif carry open crevasses; rope up with crevasse-rescue kit
Loose, rotten breccia rock on the summit block
Two-to-three-day approach with a rough spur road to the pullout
Very remote: no cell coverage and long carry-out times if a rescue is needed

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Green Mountain trail and the Horse Lake saddle

bivy.name: Horse Lake saddle camp
bivy.notes: First-night camp on the Green Mountain approach, past the south shoulder of Green Mountain. Beyond it the traverse toward Misch and Buckindy is slow sidehill travel.
bivy.water: Horse Lake and snowmelt nearby; treat it
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites just above the saddle

approachLogistics.trailhead: Green Mountain Trailhead (FR-2680 off Suiattle River Road)

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: The usual way: up the Green Mountain trail off the Suiattle River Road, then cross-country east and southeast along the ridges past Misch to Buckindy's north side. Check the Suiattle River Road before you go; it has been closed to vehicles for long stretches.
hazards: Green Mountain Road and Suiattle River Road closed to vehicles by flood damage, adding roughly twenty miles of closed road
Slow sidehill cross-country travel along the ridge system past Misch and the Horse Lake saddle
Small glaciers (Kindy and Goat Creek) on the massif carry open crevasses; rope up with crevasse-rescue kit
Loose, rotten breccia rock on the summit block
Very remote: no cell coverage and long carry-out times if a rescue is needed

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: Read the name on this route with care — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies west of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August over a buried climbers' path
Steep, slick descent off Grand Pass in wet weather or lingering snow
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the ridge connecting the three summits
Obstruction Point Road is narrow, one-lane gravel and closes for most of the year
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Exposed ridge and lightning exposure
wa_mount_cameron_standard.baseFinding: The base is Cameron Pass and the test is the direction you turn out of it: the ridge you climb rises to the east. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. Second test, and it is the one that matters most here: the ridge is a sequence of false summits. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going: the true top is still easy Class 1-2 ground, and steps of Class 3-4 mean you have passed it and are on the traverse. Third test, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. Carry a map and count your summits.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with chest-high berry bushes and log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears, with several unbridged creek branches
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the three-summit ridge
No reliable water above the basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Exposed ridge and lightning exposure
wa_mount_cameron_standard.baseFinding: Identical once you are at Cameron Pass: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground all the way to the top. The pass is west of the summit whatever the route title says. The extra test this side needs is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. What going too far looks like: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
hazards: Closed Dosewallips road adds a long walk or bike ride up the washed-out roadbed, many extra miles
Multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the three-summit ridge
Minimal to no cell coverage; long distance from help
wa_mount_cameron_standard.baseFinding: Identical at the pass: the ridge rises east out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground to the true top. The test this side needs is about which valley you are in, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first.

wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.
wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
hazards: Unreliable log crossings of the Chilliwack River; parties have lost the crossing and been forced to bushwhack
The Whatcom Glacier traverse has been found down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years
About 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing, sometimes with a short rappel across a moat, just to get off Perfect Pass onto the glacier
A bergschrund on the Challenger Glacier and a moat below the summit rocks that can be impassable late season
No bailout worth the name once you are past Whatcom Pass
wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.baseFinding:
Perfect Pass is the arrival, and you know it because the ground stops and the glacier starts. From the pass, getting down onto the Challenger Glacier at about 7,000-7,200 ft can involve roughly 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The exact entry point moves year to year with crevasse conditions, so do not look for a particular spot; look for the lowest place you can step from rock onto continuous ice.

Arrival at the climbing, which is not the same thing as arrival at the glacier: the technical climbing on this route is 50 ft long and it is the last 50 ft. Above the bergschrund the glacier steepens into a snow arete, then a clean 3rd-class scramble runs out at the base of a short, well-protected 5.5-5.7 pitch. That pitch is the route. If you are roping up anywhere lower than the foot of a single unbroken 50 ft wall with a rappel anchor visible at its top, you have roped up too early.

The moat is the marker you will meet first, and in fog it is the one that matters. Just below the summit rocks a moat has been reported up to about 5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to hunt a snow bridge. Reaching an uncrossable gap where the snow has pulled away from the summit rock means you are at the base, not lost.

What going too far looks like: continuing east along the crest away from the summit block puts you on the connecting ridge toward Poltergeist Pinnacle and Crooked Thumb, which is a different day entirely.

wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.
wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
hazards: The Impasse: deep snow moats on both sides and wet down-sloping slabs, with an 800 ft drop-and-re-climb workaround on exposed class 4
Fords of the Chilliwack River
Whiteout navigation between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, where parties have mistaken Whatcom Peak's summit wall for the pass
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier and the moat below the summit rocks
wa_mount_challenger_challenger_glacier.baseFinding:
The impasse is the checkpoint, not the base, and confusing the two is the common error in cloud. It is a notch in the ridge guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 step to regain the crest beyond.

Beyond it, the test is the same as on the other approach: Perfect Pass, then step onto ice, then keep going until the walking stops at a 50 ft rock wall. Nothing on this route is technical until that wall.

A named whiteout trap on this line: on the snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, parties in fog have headed for Whatcom Peak's summit wall instead of the pass. If the ground in front of you is steepening into a wall rather than levelling into a saddle, you are aimed at the wrong feature. Perfect Pass is a saddle with running water; Whatcom's wall has neither.

wa_mount_christie_west.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_christie_west.notes: Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 16 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
wa_mount_christie_west.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
hazards: Thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col; conditions change between seasons
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier; moat width varies by year and time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk and refreezing snow on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz bushwhacking above the col
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on the open ridge, saddle and col
Extreme remoteness: an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or helicopter
wa_mount_christie_west.baseFinding:
From lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you south — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

The confirming test is a number and a duration: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

Second test, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you drop down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the Christie Glacier. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a moat forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

What waits at the col, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.

wa_mount_christie_west.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

wa_mount_christie_west.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the November 2017 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
wa_mount_christie_west.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
hazards: Closed road adds 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike to reach Whiskey Bend
Long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
Loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier; moat width varies by year and time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
wa_mount_christie_west.baseFinding:
Identical to the Quinault variant once you are at Low Divide, and that shared test is a good one: from lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft; then down loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

The extra test this side needs is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route leaves maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.

wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.hours: 2.5-3.5 for the Lake Constance trail alone
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations for the May 15-October 15 summer season; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
hazards: fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses
steep firm snow on the Terrible Traverse - several pickets advised in early season
exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands on the Lake Constance trail above 1.3 miles
loose talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
no water above the lake in late summer, and Constance Creek itself runs dry
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.baseFinding:
From the lake, follow the boot path around the shore, out onto a large scree cone, and north into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance. A large rock called the Thumb sits on the canyon's left side; the South Chute lies on the south side of the Thumb, and due south of the Cat Ears.

The most useful rule on this mountain: start up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears come into view, not when the chute starts to look obvious. Entering low keeps you on firmer ground, where there is a path in places; parties who keep walking up the canyon and attack the chute higher get the worst of the loose scree. If the Cat Ears have been visible for a while and you are still walking north, you have overshot the entrance.

From the lake the chute line climbs roughly 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. Descend about 150 ft, then a second gully leads to a notch near 7,300 ft.

Above that is the exposed upper maze, and identifying which traverse you are on is the thing to get right. The Finger Traverse is a downsloping ledge above a cliff with old rusted pitons on it — the pitons are the identifier, and some parties clip them as a solo-belay anchor. The Terrible Traverse is a hard-snow traverse of roughly 45 degrees above a big cliff and a nasty drainage. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, ground leading to the base of the summit block. If you are on a traverse and the summit block is not visible above and ahead of you, you are on the wrong ledge.

The actual climbing is only the summit block, about 60 ft, with the North Chimney taking its north side at 3rd class — reported by plenty of people as feeling like easy 4th.

wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.notes:
The roughly 5 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the signed start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.
hazards: old roadbed surface with washouts
everything above the bike drop is unchanged, including the exposed ledges on the Lake Constance path
wa_mount_constance_north_chimney.baseFinding: Unchanged from the walk-in: around the lake, north into Avalanche Canyon, and up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears appear above you, with the Thumb on the canyon's left marking the chute's south side. The Cat Ears becoming visible is the trigger to start climbing, not a landmark to walk toward.
